content: Sanitation refers to the hygienic practices and measures aimed at preventing human contact with hazardous wastes to promote health. These hazards can include physical, microbiological, biological, or chemical agents that cause disease. Wastes that pose health risks include human and animal feces, solid wastes, domestic wastewater (such as sewage, urine, sullage, and greywater), industrial wastes, and agricultural wastes. The term sanitation can be applied to specific aspects, concepts, locations, or strategies. For example: Basic sanitation involves the management of human feces at the household level. This is a key indicator for the Millennium Development Goal on sanitation. On-site sanitation refers to the collection and treatment of waste at the location where it is deposited, such as through pit latrines, septic tanks, or Imhoff tanks. Food sanitation encompasses hygienic measures to ensure food safety. Environmental sanitation involves controlling environmental factors that contribute to disease transmission, including solid waste management, water and wastewater treatment, industrial waste treatment, and noise and pollution control. Ecological sanitation is an approach that recycles nutrients from human and animal wastes back to nature, emphasizing sustainability. Wastewater Collection In urban areas, standard sanitation technology involves collecting wastewater in sewers, treating it in wastewater treatment plants, and either reusing it or disposing of it in rivers, lakes, or the sea. Sewers may be combined with storm drains or separated as sanitary sewers. Combined sewers are often found in older urban areas. However, untreated or inadequately treated sewage can be discharged into the environment, posing risks. Industrial wastewater is often discharged into municipal sewers, which can complicate treatment unless pre-treatment is performed. The high costs of conventional wastewater collection systems make them unaffordable for many developing countries, leading to the promotion of alternative systems like condominial sewerage, which uses smaller diameter pipes at shallower depths. Wastewater Treatment In developed countries, municipal wastewater treatment is widespread but not universal. In contrast, most wastewater in developing countries is discharged untreated into the environment. For instance, in Latin America, only about 15% of collected sewage is treated. Reuse of Wastewater In developing countries, untreated wastewater is commonly reused for irrigated agriculture. Treated wastewater is increasingly reused for landscaping (e.g., on golf courses), irrigated agriculture, and industrial purposes. In peri-urban and rural areas, many households are not connected to sewers and instead use septic tanks or other on-site sanitation systems. Ecological Sanitation Ecological sanitation is sometimes proposed as a radical alternative to conventional systems. It involves separating urine and feces at the source for sanitation and recycling purposes, thereby eliminating fecal pathogens from the wastewater flow. If implemented, municipal wastewater would consist primarily of greywater, which can be recycled for gardening. However, in most cases, greywater continues to be discharged into sewers. Sanitation and Public Health The isolation of waste is critical to preventing waterand sanitation-related diseases, which affect both developed and developing countries to varying degrees. It is estimated that up to 5 million people die annually from preventable waterborne diseases due to inadequate sanitation and hygiene practices. Global Access to Improved Sanitation The WHO and UNICEF Joint Monitoring Program defines improved sanitation as access to facilities such as: Connection to a public sewer Connection to a septic system Pour-flush latrines Simple pit latrines Ventilated improved pit latrines As of 2004, 59% of the global population had access to improved sanitation, but only 31% lived in homes connected to a sewer. Approximately 2.6 billion people lacked access to improved sanitation, resorting to open defecation or unsanitary facilities, which poses significant public health risks, including contamination of drinking water and life-threatening diarrhea in infants. In developed countries, where less than 20% of the global population resides, 99% have access to improved sanitation, and 81% are connected to sewers. Solid Waste Disposal Solid waste is most commonly disposed of in landfills, but incineration, recycling, composting, and conversion to biofuels are also practiced. Advanced countries typically enforce strict protocols for daily landfill cover with topsoil to reduce vector contact, pathogen spread, odor emissions, and windblown litter. They also require perimeter sealing of landfills with clay-type soils to minimize leachate migration, which could contaminate groundwater. Incineration, while effective, can release air pollutants, including toxic components. Recycling and biofuel conversion are sustainable options with superior life-cycle costs, especially when ecological consequences are considered. Composting is limited by market demand for compost products. Sanitation in the Food Industry In the food industry, sanitation involves adequately treating food-contact surfaces to destroy vegetative cells of microorganisms of public health significance and substantially reduce other undesirable microorganisms without compromising product safety or quality. In the food and biopharmaceutical industries, sanitary equipment refers to equipment that is fully cleanable using Clean-in-Place (CIP) and Sterilization-in-Place (SIP) procedures. Such equipment must be fully drainable and designed to minimize areas where cleaning turbulence is insufficient to remove product deposits. Stainless steel 316L, with a surface finish of less than 0.5 micrometers, is commonly used to reduce bacterial adhesion. History of Sanitation The earliest evidence of urban sanitation systems was found in the Indus Valley civilization, including Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and Rakhigarhi. These cities featured advanced urban planning with covered drains lining major streets and waste management systems. In Europe, sanitation systems were largely absent until the High Middle Ages. Unsanitary conditions were widespread during the Middle Ages, but the catastrophic effects of poor sanitation became evident during the 14th century when overcrowding and lack of sanitation contributed to the Black Death, which killed 25 million Europeans. High infant and child mortality rates persisted in medieval Europe due to poor sanitation and insufficient food supplies. Sanitation and food supply were critical factors in balancing population growth during the period from 1300 to 1600, particularly in urban areas.
